American Business.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain four features of the free enterprise system in the United States. Describe the difference between freedom and license. Tell how the Scout Oath and Scout Law apply to business and free enterprise. (b) Describe the Industrial Revolution and tell about the major developments that marked the start of the modern industrial era in the United States. Discuss three people who had a great influence on business or industry in the United States and describe what each did. (c) Identify and describe to your counselor the five primary areas of business. (d) Explain the history of labor unions in the United States and the importance of labor unions and employers working together. Identify two major labor unions currently in existence. (e) Discuss with your counselor how business impacts the local, national, and global economy.

They Organized: They organized associationsthat promoted industrialization.
Than Three-fourths: Although more than three-fourths of the workingpopulation in the United States was involved in agriculture atthe time, the Industrial Revolution spread.
End Century United: By the end of the century, the United Statesbecame the world leader in manufacturing and spurred what isknown as the Second Industrial Revolution.
step_by_step_procedure: United Statescontinues: The United Statescontinues to be one of the world's largest producers of goods.
Result Globalization: The result of globalization is a worldeconomy in which the borders between countries have blurred.
Technology Internet Helped: Technology, such as the internet, has helped makeglobal corporations and m ­ arkets possible.
Globalization Grown Rapidly: Globalization has grown rapidly since the 1970s, but it hasbeen an economic trend since the end of World War II in 1945.

pamphlet_excerpts: Business Contracts Formal: Many business contracts are formal and complicated.
Othercontracts Informal: Othercontracts are informal and hardly noticeable.
Business Transaction Simple: Every business transaction, from one as simple asbuying a snack to one as complex as a company issuing stock, is a contract of some type.
Partytrusts She Promised: Each partytrusts the other to do what he or she has promised.
step_by_step_procedure: Financial Statements: Financial statements for businesses usually include incomestatements, balance sheets, statements of retained earnings, andstatements of cash flows.
Financialstatements Audited: Financialstatements are often audited by government agencies, accountants, firms, and other entities to ensure accuracy and for tax.
Main Financialstatements: The three main financialstatements are the balance sheet, income statement, and cashflow statement.
Balance Sheet Provides: The balance sheet provides an overview of assets, liabilities, andshareholders’ equity as a snapshot in time.

American Heritage.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Select two individuals from American history, one a political leader (a president, senator, etc.) and the other a private citizen (a writer, religious leader, etc.). Find out about each person's accomplishments and compare the contributions each has made to America's heritage. (b) With your counselor's approval, choose an organization that has promoted some type of positive change in American society. Find out why the organization believed this change was necessary and how it helped to accomplish the change. Discuss how this organization is related to events or situations from America's past. (c) With your counselor's approval, interview two veterans of the U.S. military. Find out what their experiences were like. Ask the veterans what they believe they accomplished. (d) With your counselor's approval, interview three people in your community of different ages and occupations. Ask these people what America means to them, what they think is special about this country, and what American traditions they feel are important to preserve.

American Heritage.req_text: Do the following: (a) Select a topic related to the United States that is currently in the news. Describe to your counselor what is happening. Explain how today's events are related to or affected by the events and values of America's past. (b) For the following, describe its adoption, tell about any changes since its adoption, and explain how each one continues to influence Americans today: the flag, the Pledge of Allegiance, the Great Seal of the United States, the motto, and the national anthem. (c) Research your family's history. Find out how various events and situations in American history affected your family. If your family immigrated to America, tell the reasons why. Share what you find with your counselor.

Reflection America Heritage: It is more of a reflection of America’s heritage, in which religion has played a role.

American Heritage.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Explain the National Register of Historic Places and how a property becomes eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places. Make a map of your local area, marking the points of historical interest. Tell about any National Register properties in your area. Share the map with your counselor, and describe the historical points you have indicated. (b) Research an event of historical importance that took place in or near your area. If possible, visit the place. Tell your counselor about the event and how it affected local history. Describe how the area looked then and what it now looks like. (c) Find out when, why, and how your town or neighborhood started, and what ethnic, national, or racial groups played a part. Find out how the area has changed over the past 50 years and try to explain why. (d) Take an active part in a program about an event or person in American history. Report to your counselor about the program, the part you took, and the subject. (e) Visit a historic trail or walk in your area. After your visit, share with your counselor what you have learned. Discuss the importance of this location and explain why you think it might qualify for National Register listing.

There Specific Criteria: There are very specific criteria for a property to be listed.
Aboveall Property: Aboveall, the property must be significant in American history, architecture, archaeology, and culture.
Once Foundwhat National: Once you have foundwhat National Register properties arein your area, plot them on a map.
step_by_step_procedure: Map Does Not: Your map does not have to be exact, but it should identify major streets, highways, and natural resources suchas lakes and rivers.
Local Library Chamber: Your local library, chamber of commerce, or realty officemight be able to provide you with amap of your town.
City Websitealso Link: Your city’s websitealso may have a link to a map youcan print out; just plug in the townand state name in your browser tobegin the search.
Than Listings There: With more than 77,000 listings, there is a good chance aproperty in your town is listed on the National Register.

American Heritage.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Watch two motion pictures (with the approval and permission of your counselor and parent or guardian) that are set in some period of American history. Describe to your counselor how accurate each film is with regard to the historical events depicted and also with regard to the way the characters are portrayed. (b) Read a biography (with your counselor's approval) of someone who has made a contribution to America's heritage. Tell some things you admire about this individual and some things you do not admire. Explain why you think this person has made a positive or a negative contribution to America's heritage. (c) Listen to recordings of popular songs from various periods of American history. Share five of these songs with your counselor, and describe how each song reflects the way people felt about the period in which it was popular. If a recording is not available, have a copy of the lyrics available.

pamphlet_excerpts: Us and Them: The Struggles Between Labor and Management.
Big Business Fought: Big business fought union efforts to have any influencein the workplace.
Management Courts Private: Management used the courts, private armies, and federal troops to put down labor activity.
Employers Contracted Prisons: Employers contracted with prisons to hire convicts as strikebreakers.
step_by_step_procedure: Additionally Employers Hired: Additionally, employers hired new immigrants, African Americans, and Latinosto break strikes, often causing racial unrest.
Trade Unionism Grewin: Trade unionism grewin fits and starts in response to the success or failure of strikes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and union militancy.
Labor Movement Century: The Labor Movement in the 20th Century Labor leaders promoted the ideas of union solidarity (a spiritof unity based on common interests).
However Deep-rooted: However, deep-rooted prejudice and fear oftenexerted a stronger influence on union members than idealism.

Animal Science.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
Animal Science.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A—Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf. (b) Option B—Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings. (c) Option C—Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. (5) Outline the proper feeding of a horse doing light work. Explain why the amount and kind of feed will change according to the kind of horse and the work it does. Describe what colic is, what can cause it, and its symptoms. (d) Option D—Sheep or Goat. Choose one and do ALL of the following based upon the choice: (1) Make a sketch of a live lamb or goat. Show the location of the various wholesale and retail cuts. (2) Discuss how wools are sorted and graded. (3) List products that can be made from the milk. (4) Based on your choice, do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm or ranch where sheep or goats are raised. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on sheep or goats. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms for a sheep (wether, ewe, ram, and lamb) OR a goat (doe, nanny, kid, buck, and billy). (e) Option E—Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar. (f) Option F—Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

sub_requirements.label: (a)
sub_requirements.text: Option A—Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C—Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C—Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. (5) Outline the proper feeding of a horse doing light work. Explain why the amount and kind of feed will change according to the kind of horse and the work it does. Describe what colic is, what can cause it, and its symptoms.

sub_requirements.label: (d)
sub_requirements.text: Option D—Sheep or Goat. Choose one and do ALL of the following based upon the choice: (1) Make a sketch of a live lamb or goat. Show the location of the various wholesale and retail cuts. (2) Discuss how wools are sorted and graded. (3) List products that can be made from the milk. (4) Based on your choice, do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm or ranch where sheep or goats are raised. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on sheep or goats. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms for a sheep (wether, ewe, ram, and lamb) OR a goat (doe, nanny, kid, buck, and billy).

sub_requirements.label: (f)
sub_requirements.text: Option F—Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

step_by_step_procedure: Kind Entertainment Beenjoyed: This kind of entertainment can beenjoyed by a group of friends.

Primitive Projection: A primitive projection devicelike a wooden box with a candle inside was fitted with a lens.

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles Animation Basic: The principles of animation are a set of 12 basic ideas applied toanimation to create appealing, believable results.
They Wereintroduced Original: They wereintroduced by two of the original Disney animators, Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas, in their book, Disney Animation: The Illusion.
Since Time Principles: Since that time, the principles havebecome standard in the animation industry.
Straight Ahead Action: Straight Ahead Action and Pose to Pose Straight-ahead action and pose to pose are the two mainmethods for animating.
step_by_step_procedure: Straight-ahead Action: Using straight-ahead action, theanimator draws or animates frame by frame, doing the drawingsin order: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on.
Pose-to-pose Animation: With pose-to-pose animation, incontrast, the animator draws or poses the main (key) frames ofthe animation before filling in the in-between.
Thepose-to-pose Method: Using thepose-to-pose method, the animator might do drawing 1, thendrawing 25, and then drawing 47, before going back to do thedrawings.
Animators Pose-to-pose: Most animators use the pose-to-pose method becauseit offers benefits in timing and frame composition.

Archaeologists Walk: Archaeologists walk the entirearea, looking for anything made by humans that is more than 50 years old.
They Dig Test: They may dig test pits or trenches in the pathwayof the proposed construction.
Artifacts Appear Site: If artifacts appear, the site may be excavated beforeconstruction machinery disturbs the area.

Think Little Parts: Think of all the little parts that go together to make asmartphone.
Individual Parts Out: If you take the individual parts out of a smartphoneand study each one separately, will that tell you how the phonefunctions?.
Parts Insidethe Phone: You must look at all of the parts in place insidethe phone to see how they work together.
step_by_step_procedure: Smartphone Archaeological: Like a smartphone, an archaeological site is a complicated package that must be opened carefully and studiedas a whole if we are to make sense.
Researcher Looks Few: A researcher who looks at only a few stone tools and afew kernels of corn might find that, by themselves, the artifactsreveal little.
Few Kernels Corn: A few kernels of corn found in a spacethat did not have a hearth or any other artifacts would suggestthat the room was probably a storeroom.
Compared Anisolated: Compared with anisolated find, artifacts foundtogether at a sitecan provide moreinformation aboutthe people wholived there andeveryday activitiesof.

Archaeology.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission, assist a qualified archaeologist for at least eight hours with a project being worked on. Projects may include surveying, site monitoring, site stabilization, surface excavation, laboratory analysis, use of digital archaeological technology, or public outreach. Describe your involvement in the project, what you learned about archaeology, and the steps of archaeological inquiry. Note: Visiting an archaeological site will require advance planning. An archaeological site during study can be a dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the archaeologist's directions and comply with all the safety procedures. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site. (b) With your counselor's approval, take part in a simulated archaeological project designed by a qualified archaeologist. The project must include the use of a simulated archaeological site including artifacts and features for the site. Using the steps of archaeological inquiry, analyze the artifacts and features and document the spatial relationships of the artifacts and features at the simulated site. Explain how the environment and time can affect the interpretation of an artifact and the overall archaeological site. Tell how you would share the results of your analysis with other researchers and the public. Note: To find out how to make a simulated archaeological site, talk with a professional archaeologist, trained avocational archaeologist, museum school instructor, science teacher, advisor from a local archaeology society, or other qualified instructor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Whistle Commands Range: The whistle commands used on a range, and their relatedverbal commands, are as follows.
Blasts Whistle Shootingline: Two blasts on a whistle, ”Step to the shootingline.” You may step to the shooting line and pick upyour bow.
Blast Whistle Commence: One blast on a whistle, ”Commence shooting.” You may pick up an arrow and shoot this end.
Whenyou Done Bow: Whenyou are done, put your bow in a bow stand and stepto the waiting line. 3.
step_by_step_procedure: Blasts Whistle Retrieve: Three blasts on a whistle, ”Retrieve your arrows.” You may go downrange and retrieve your arrows.
Follow Rules Retrieving: Follow the three rules for retrieving arrows (above). 4.
Blasts Whistle STOP: Four or more blasts on a whistle, ”STOP!” or “Cease fire!” Do not shoot.
However Way Transportan: However, the best way to transportan arrow is safely in its quiver. • Be sure the area around and beyond your target is clearbefore you shoot.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While shooting on the archery range, an arrow slips off your bow rest and lands on the ground 4 feet in front of the shooting line while other archers are still at full draw. What must you do?
options: Lean forward across the shooting line and grab the arrow quickly before anyone notices.
Leave the arrow on the ground, never reach or step across the shooting line while the range is hot, and wait for the Range Officer's three-whistle 'Retrieve Arrows' command.
Signal your buddy in the next lane to kick the arrow back behind the waiting line.
quiz_item.correct_answer: Option B — Leave the dropped arrow untouched in front of the shooting line until the Range Officer blows three whistles to retrieve arrows.
quiz_item.explanation: Stepping or reaching across an active shooting line puts you directly in the path of adjacent bows; any arrow forward of the line is retrieved only after all bows are racked on the 3-whistle signal.

pamphlet_excerpts: Tell Arrows Apart: You also can tell arrows apart by their fletchings. • Target arrows use small fletchings.
Feathersfrom Inches Long: These can be feathersfrom 2 to 3 inches long or plastic vanes about 11/2 to 2 inches long.
Fletchings Blunt-tipped: These fletchings are most often used on blunt-tipped arrows.
They Slow Arrow: They slow the arrow’s flight and make it drop quickly. • Hunting arrows use longer fletchings, usually 4 to 5 incheslong.
step_by_step_procedure: Fletchings Strong Spiral: The fletchings usually have a strong spiral that causesthe arrow to rotate, which improves its flight when the pointis a broadhead.
Modern Arrow Shafts: Modern arrow shafts are made from four principal materials: wood, aluminum, fiberglass, or carbon fiber.
Beginning Archersusually: Beginning archersusually use arrows with wood shafts.
Wood Least Expensive: Wood is the least expensive shaft material and is popular with many archers.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hunting Arm Guard: The hunting arm guard usually is wider and longer thanguards used on field and target ranges.
Protect Shooting Fingers: Protect your shooting fingers with a shooting glove or tab.
Lightest Bow Soon: Even the lightest bow will soon make untrained fingerssensitive, eventually causing blisters.
Archers Usefinger Protection: All archers should usefinger protection, no matter how tough they think their fingersare.
step_by_step_procedure: Experienced Skilled Archers: The most experienced and skilled archers always shootwith a glove or tab.
Without Gloveor Tab: Without a gloveor tab, the releaseof your arrow, which is the mostcrucial motion inshooting, maybe faulty.

Differenttarget Faces: Differenttarget faces and shooting distances are used for 14 targets.
Stakes Driven Ground: Stakes driven into the ground mark the exact shooting spotfor each target.
Outdoor Target Archery: Outdoor target archery is set up in an open field, using 122-centimeter (48-inch) target faces.
step_by_step_procedure: Cases Targetposition: In most cases, the targetposition is set and the shooting line is moved when differentdistances are shot.
Indoor Target Archery: Indoor target archery is shot in a building, using 60- or 40-centimeter targets at a distance of 18 meters (20 yards).
Target Archers Straddle: Target archers straddle the firing line, with one foot in frontof and one foot behind the line.
Organizations Govern Archery: These four organizations govern archery tournaments.

Archery.lead_text: Working under the supervision of a certified USA Archery Level 1 Instructor or a certified long-term camp staff member (i.e., a National Camping School [NCS] Range Activities Director; or a Rangemaster over age 18 who is trained by an NCS Range Activities Director or by a USA Archery Level 1 Instructor), do ONE of the following options: Note: When using a Genesis bow, apply the requirements in Option A.
Archery.req_text: Working under the supervision of a certified USA Archery Level 1 Instructor or a certified long-term camp staff member (i.e., a National Camping School [NCS] Range Activities Director; or a Rangemaster over age 18 who is trained by an NCS Range Activities Director or by a USA Archery Level 1 Instructor), do ONE of the following options: Note: When using a Genesis bow, apply the requirements in Option A. (a) Option A—Recurve Bow or Longbow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the recurve or longbow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store recurve bows and longbows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Demonstrate the proper way to string a recurve bow or longbow. (5) Using a bow square, locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a recurve bow or longbow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 60 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 80 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 80 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 50 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting 30 arrows in five-arrow ends at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target at 10 yards and using the 10 scoring regions, make a score of 150 points. (b) Option B—Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

(b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

Architecture.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and approval, arrange to meet with an architect. Ask to see the scale model of a building and the drawings that a builder would use to construct this building. Discuss why the different building materials were selected. Look at the details in the drawings and the model to see how the materials and components are attached to each other during construction. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and approval, arrange to meet with an architect at a construction site. Ask the architect to bring drawings that the builder uses to construct the building. While at the site, discuss why the different building materials being used were selected. Discuss how the different building materials and components are attached to each other during construction. Note: To visit a construction site will require advance planning. You will need permission from a parent or guardian, counselor, the architect, and the construction site manager. A construction site is a very dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the site manager's directions and comply with all the safety procedures, including wearing a hard hat, protective eyewear, and proper footwear. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site, and stay with the architect or site manager. (c) Interview someone who might be your client (such as a prospective homeowner or business owner) if you were an architect. Find out what your client's requirements would be for designing a new home or business building. Write a short program including a list of requirements for the project, the functions of the building and site, how the functions relate to one another, and the goals of the project.

pamphlet_excerpts: Elements Art Design: Elements of Art and Design Balance Balance is the visual stability of the composition.
Workof Art Visual: If a workof art has visual balance, then the viewer feels that the elements have been arranged just right.
There Imbalance Then: If there is an imbalance, then the viewer feels something’s wrong, that the elementsneed to be rearranged.
Formal Balance Occurs: A formal balance occurs whensimilar elements are placed on eachside of the central axis (a drawn orimaginary line through the centerof the work).
step_by_step_procedure: Differentelements Art Line: The differentelements of art, line, value, shape, space, color, and texture, all influencethe visual weight of a composition.
Forexample Small Area: Forexample, a small area of bright colorcan balance a larger area of dull color.
Art Design Elements: Elements of Art and Design Elements of Artand Design When you create art, you are expressing your ideas, your feelings, or your beliefs.
Intend Share Art: If you intend to share your art with otherpeople, you need to know how to organize your design so thatthey will understand what your art is telling.

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles Guidelines: These principles are guidelines, notrules, to help you express yourself artistically.
Understandingthese Principles: Understandingthese principles also will help you to appreciate how other artists try to communicate through their work.
Six Principles Design: The six principles of design are rhythm, balance, proportion, variety, emphasis, and unity.
Rhythm Indicates Movement: Rhythm indicates movement by the repetition of a certain artelement or combination of elements.
step_by_step_procedure: Repeated Element Shape: The repeated element, a shape or line, for example, is called a motif.
Artistuses Repetition Motif: The artistuses the repetition of a motif to lead the viewer’s eye aroundthe work of art.
Random Rhythm Happenswhen: Random rhythm happenswhen a motif is repeated in noapparent order, with irregularspacing between one motifand the next.
Regular Rhythm Occurs: Regular rhythm occurs whenidentical motifs with identicalspacing between them arerepeated.

pamphlet_excerpts: Artists Line Color: Artists use line and color in different ways to make paintings.
Artwork Line Drawing: In some artwork, the line drawing is the basis for the paintingand color is a secondary element, added to describe the outlined forms.
Works Color Subject: In other works, color is the subject of the painting.
Matter Plan Color: No matter how you plan to use color, you need to knowhow to mix pigments and apply the paint.
step_by_step_procedure: Paint Formed Pigment: Paint is formed when a pigment is mixed with a bindingmedium.
Pigment Finely Ground: Pigment is finely ground, colored powder that comesfrom natural sources like minerals and plants or from chemicals.
Binding Medium Liquid: Binding medium is a liquid substance that holds pigment particles together and attaches them to a surface.
Substance Isalso Vehicle: This substance isalso called a vehicle because it “carries” the pigment.

Artificial Intelligence.lead_text: Practical Application. Do ONE of the following:
Artificial Intelligence.req_text: Practical Application. Do ONE of the following: (a) With your counselor's approval, choose an artificial intelligence project based on your personal interest or a community need. Develop a plan outlining the project's objectives, data requirements, and potential ethical considerations. Implement the project utilizing appropriate artificial intelligence tools, languages, or platforms. Share your project with your counselor. Discuss the steps you followed to create the project and your experience during the process. (b) With your counselor's approval, design a short lesson plan on AI and teach it to your patrol or a group of Scouts. pamphlet_excerpts: Move Victim Ashelter: Move the victim to ashelter, remove damp clothing, and warm the person withblankets until body temperature returns to normal.
Cover Thehead Warm: Cover thehead with a warm hat or other covering, and offer hot drinks.
Condition Progresses: If the condition progresses, actively warm the victim’s body.
Victim Sleeping Bag: Place the victim into a sleeping bag with one or two other people.
step_by_step_procedure: Stripped Clothing: All should be stripped of most clothing so that skin-to-skincontact can hasten the warming, and perhaps save a life.
Severe Hypothermia Requires: Severe hypothermia requires immediate medical attention.
Cold Weather Wear: In cold weather, wear layers to keep in the heat.
Bring Along Woolen: Bring along a woolen cap, scarf, gloves, extra socks, and a coat.

Astronomy.lead_text: Do the following (if instruction is done in a planetarium, Scouts must still identify the required stars and constellations outside under the natural night sky):
Astronomy.req_text: Do the following (if instruction is done in a planetarium, Scouts must still identify the required stars and constellations outside under the natural night sky): (a) Identify in the sky 10 constellations, at least four of which are in the zodiac. (b) Identify in the sky eight conspicuous stars, five of which are of magnitude 1 or brighter. (c) Make two sketches of the Big Dipper or Cassiopeia from direct observation. In one sketch, show the Big Dipper's or Cassiopeia's orientation in the early evening sky. Make another sketch, showing its position several hours later. In both sketches, show the North Star and the horizon. Record the date and time each sketch was made. (d) Explain what we see when we look at the Milky Way.

pamphlet_excerpts: Venus Appears Early: Venus also appears only in the early evening or earlymorning sky, but it is much easier to see than Mercury.
Morning Evening Star: Sometimes called the morning or the evening star, diamondwhite and brilliant Venus is the brightest planet as seen fromthe Earth.
Venus Evening Sky: If Venus is in the evening sky, you can’t miss it.
Different Parts Their: Because different parts of their sunlit areas are visiblefrom Earth at different times, Mercury and Venus have phasessimilar to the Moon’s.
step_by_step_procedure: Different Times They: At different times, they appear full, gibbous (three-quarters full), half-full (like a first-quarter or lastquarter moon), as a crescent.
Mercury Venus Same: When Mercury or Venus is on the same side of the Sun as Earth, the planet’s unlit side faces Earth.
Planet Movesaround Sun: As the planet movesaround the Sun away from Earth, its sunlit side becomes visible as a thin crescent and grows gradually as the planet.
Mercury Venus Near: When Mercury or Venus is near the other side of the Sun, we can see almost all of its sunlit face, the full phase.

(b) Sketch the phase and position of the Moon, at the same hour and place, for four nights (or days) within a one-week period by direct observation. (d) With the aid of diagrams, explain the relative positions of the Sun, Earth, and the Moon at the times of lunar and solar eclipses, and at the times of new, first-quarter, full, and last-quarter phases of the Moon.

Earth Nebulae Giant: From Earth, we can see nebulae, or giant clouds of gas and dust.
Rare Seesights Meteor: Sometimes it is rare to seesights like meteor showers or dramatic eclipses.
Learning Astronomy Study: In learning about astronomy, you will study how activitiesin space affect your own planet.
step_by_step_procedure: Daily Schedule Daytimeand: Your daily schedule, daytimeand nighttime, is dictated by Earth’s rotation.
Earth Orbitaround Sun: Earth’s orbitaround the Sun takes a year and gives us the changing seasons.
Sun Energy Affects: The Sun’s energy affects the weather, and the gravitational pullbetween Earth and the Moon creates and controls ocean tides.
Wasn NASA Kepler: It wasn’t until 2011 that NASA’s Kepler spacecraft discovered two Earth-sizedplanets beyond the solar system.

Astronomy.lead_text: With your counselor's approval and guidance, do ONE of the following:
Astronomy.req_text: With your counselor's approval and guidance, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a planetarium or astronomical observatory. Submit a written report, a scrapbook, OR a video presentation afterward to your counselor that includes the following information: activities occurring there, exhibits and displays you saw, telescopes and other instruments being used, and celestial objects you observed. (b) Plan and participate in an observation session that includes using binoculars or a telescope and includes at least 10 celestial objects beyond those observed in requirement 4. These might be lunar features, Messier objects, additional constellations or planets, or artificial satellites including the International Space Station. List the celestial objects you want to observe and find each in a star chart, guidebook or by using an app. Prepare a log or notebook. Discuss with your counselor what you hope to observe prior to your observation session. Review your log or notebook with your counselor afterward. (c) Plan and host a star party for your Scout troop or other group such as your class at school. Use binoculars or a telescope to show and explain celestial objects to the group. (d) Help an astronomy club in your community hold a star party that is open to the public. (e) Personally take a series of photographs or digital images of the movement of the Moon, a planet, an asteroid, meteor, or a comet. In your visual display, label each image and include the date and time it was taken. Show all positions on a star chart or map. Show your display at school or at a troop meeting. Explain the changes you observed. (f) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, use online observing opportunities such as SkyNet to observe planets, comets, galaxies, and/or the sun. Describe your experience to your counselor.

Element Hydrogen Oxygen: Each element, such as hydrogen, oxygen, or carbon, gives offor absorbs particular colors of light.
Unique Color Patterncan: So the unique color patterncan be used to identify the elements that make up the object.
Colors Shifted Slightly: The colors can be shifted slightly if the object is moving towardor away from the Earth.
step_by_step_procedure: Thus Spectrum Usedto: Thus, a spectrum can also be usedto measure the speed with which objects are approaching orreceding from us.
Astronomical Photography: Astronomical photography allows you to keep a record of yourobservations of the sky and to share your experiences withfriends and family.
Modern Digital Cameras: Modern digital cameras are very sensitiveto light, and objects appear brighter and clearer in photographsthan through a telescope or binoculars.

Astronomy.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in astronomy. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in astronomy to pursue a personal hobby. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a warm afternoon track practice for the 1,500-meter run, a Scout stops sweating, becomes confused and unsteady, and has hot, flushed skin. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid action?
options: Have the Scout jog two slow cool-down laps around the track while sipping a sports drink.
Recognize life-threatening heatstroke: call 911 immediately, move the Scout into shade, remove excess layers, and rapidly cool the body with cold water or ice packs at the neck, armpits, and groin.
Wrap the Scout in a warm fleece blanket to prevent chills and wait 30 minutes before notifying the counselor.
quiz_item.correct_answer: Option B — Call 911 immediately and begin rapid active cooling in the shade.
quiz_item.explanation: Hot skin combined with altered mental status (confusion or dizziness) during exertion indicates heatstroke, a medical emergency requiring immediate EMS activation and aggressive cooling per the Athletics Merit Badge Pamphlet.

Athletics.lead_text: Complete the activities in FOUR of the following options and show improvement over a three-month period:
Athletics.req_text: Complete the activities in FOUR of the following options and show improvement over a three-month period: (a) Option A—Sprinting. Do ALL of the following: (1) 100-meter dash (2) 200-meter dash (b) Option B—Long-Distance Running. Do ALL of the following: (1) 3k run (2) 5k run (c) Option C—Long Jump OR High Jump. Do ALL of the following: (1) Running long jump OR running high jump (best of three tries) (2) Standing long jump OR standing high jump (best of three tries) (d) Option D—Swimming. Do ALL of the following: (1) 100-meter swim (2) 200-meter swim (e) Option E—Pull-Ups AND Push-Ups. Do ALL of the following: (1) Pull-ups in two minutes (2) Push-ups in two minutes (f) Option F—Baseball Throw. Do ALL of the following: (1) Baseball throw for accuracy, 10 throws at a target (distance to be determined by age): ages 11 to 12, 20 feet; ages 13 to 15, 30 feet; ages 16 to 17, 40 feet (2) Baseball throw for distance, five throws (total distance) (g) Option G—Basketball Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Basketball shot for accuracy, 10 free-throw shots (2) Basketball throw for skill and agility, the following shots: (a) Left-side layup (b) Right-side layup (c) Left side of hoop, along the key line (d) Right side of hoop, along the key line (e) Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side (f) Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side (g) Top of the key (h) Another spot along the three-point line (h) Option H—Football Kick OR Soccer Kick. Do ALL of the following: (1) Goals from the 10-yard line, eight kicks (2) Football kick or soccer kick for distance, five kicks (total distance) (i) Option I—Weight Training. Do ALL of the following: (1) Chest/bench press, two sets of 15 repetitions each (2) Leg curls, two sets of 15 repetitions each

Basketball Throw Skill: Basketball throw for skill and agility (see the basketball key diagram provided) 1.
Key Line Free-throw: Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side 6.
Line Free-throw Line: Where key line and free-throw line meet, right side 7.
step_by_step_procedure: Warm Upyour Arm: Before you startto throw, warm upyour arm graduallyby throwing yourbaseball atslow speed tosomeone at aclose distance.
Remember Warm Stretch: Remember to warm up and stretch before you begin.
Start Few Short: Start with a few short and easy throws, then gradually build up distanceand speed during your workouts.
Especially Towork Closely: It is especially important towork closely with your coach on your form.

Automotive Maintenance.lead_text: Safety and Registration. Do the following:
Automotive Maintenance.req_text: Safety and Registration. Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the hazards you are most likely to encounter during automotive maintenance activities, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, or lessen these hazards. (b) Discuss with your counselor the safety equipment, tools, and clothing used while checking or repairing a motor vehicle. Use this equipment, tools, and/or clothing (when needed or called for) in meeting the requirements for this merit badge. (c) Explain the different ways motor vehicles are powered. (d) Explain the safety considerations when performing maintenance on a vehicle equipped with a high-voltage electrical system. (e) Review the maintenance chart in the vehicle owner's manual. Explain the requirements and time limits. (f) Explain the purpose, importance, and limitations of safety belts and passive restraints. (g) Find out the requirements for your state's emissions and safety inspections (as applicable), including how often a vehicle needs to be inspected. (h) Explain the importance of registering a vehicle and find out the annual registration fee for renewing your family car's registration.

Do the following: (a) Demonstrate how to check the following: (1) Brake fluid (2) Engine oil (3) Coolant (4) Power steering fluid (5) Windshield washer fluid (6) Transmission fluid (7) Battery fluid (if possible) and condition of the battery terminals (b) Locate the fuse boxes; determine the type and size of fuses. Demonstrate the proper replacement of burned-out fuses. (c) Demonstrate how to check the condition and tension of belts and hoses. (d) Check the vehicle for proper operation of its lights, including the interior overhead lights, instrument lights, warning lights, and exterior bulbs. (e) Locate and check the air filter(s).

Accurately Checkthe Tension: To accurately checkthe tension of belts, you must use abelt tension gauge.
However Canget Rough: However, you canget a rough idea oftension by depressing the belt in themiddle of its longeststraight section.
Modernserpentine Belts Donot: Modernserpentine belts donot show obviouswear; use amanufacturerapproved weargauge to determineif replacementis needed.
step_by_step_procedure: Engine Internal Systems: While keeping the engine and other internal systems is vitalin extending the life of a car, don’t forget to maintain the car’soutside.
Older-model Cars Painted: Most older-model cars were painted with a clear-coatfinish that protects the metal or fiberglass car body andprovides an attractive shine.
Clear-coat Colors Areeasily: Clear-coat colors also areeasily matched if one panel of the car must be replaced afteran accident.
Commercialcar Wash Product: If you use a commercialcar wash product, follow the instructions on the bottle and besure to use plenty of water to rinse the car completely.

Automotive Maintenance.req_text: Dashboard/Driver Information Center. (b) Explain the symbols that light up on the dashboard and the difference between the yellow and red symbols. Explain each of the indicators on the dashboard, using the owner's manual if necessary. (c) Explain the messages and alerts that may be displayed on the dashboard/driver information center including maintenance-related reminders.

Check Them Off: Check them off as youidentify them. ■ Malfunction indicator lamp (MIL).
Indicator Oftencalled Check: This indicator is oftencalled the “check engine” light.
Comes Theengine Emissions: It comes on if one of theengine’s emissions control systems may have a problem.
step_by_step_procedure: Vehicle Drives Normally: Even if the vehicle drives normally, the problem couldreduce fuel economy and cause increased emissions. ■ Charging system indicator.
Indicator Tells Thebattery: This indicator tells you that thebattery is not charging properly.
Comes Vehicle Qualified: If it comes on, take the vehicle to a qualified shop as soon as possible. ■ Oil pressure gauge.
Gauge Shows Engine: This gauge shows the engine oil pressure in pounds per square inch (PSI).

(b) Demonstrate how to check tire pressure and properly inflate a tire. Check the spare tire and make sure it is ready for use. (c) Explain why wheel alignment is important to the life of a tire. (e) Explain how to dispose of old tires in accordance with local laws and regulations.

pamphlet_excerpts: Electric Vehicle Works: An electric vehicle (EV) works differently than a traditionalgasoline car.
Instead Internal Combustion: Instead of using an internal combustion enginethat runs on gasoline, an EV uses an electric motor powered byelectricity stored in a large battery.
Battery: EVs have a big battery pack, usually located under thefloor or in the back of the car.
Battery Stores Electricity: This battery stores electricity, much like how your phone stores power.
step_by_step_procedure: Battery Chargedby Plugging: The battery is chargedby plugging it into a charging station or a wall outlet. 2.
Electric Motor: The electric motor in an EV is like the enginein a regular car, but it runs on electricity.
Onthe Accelerator Pedal: When you step onthe accelerator pedal, the electric motor receives electricityfrom the battery and uses it to generate motion.
Controller: The controller manages the flow of electricityfrom the battery to the electric motor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Manufacturers Generally: Manufacturers generally recommend an equal mixture of waterand ethylene-glycol antifreeze.
Coolant Mixture Offers: This coolant mixture offers goodcooling during the summer and protects the engine down toabout 35 degrees below zero Fahrenheit in the winter.
Youuse Type Coolant: When youuse this type of coolant, you should not add water.
Coolant Checked Regularly: Coolant should be checked regularly and replaced about every 30,000 miles or two years, or up to five years in some newervehicles.
step_by_step_procedure: System Flushed There: The system also might need to be flushed if there is toomuch dirt and rust in the coolant.
Check Car Coolant: To check the car’s coolant in most new cars, you needonly to check the coolant level on the plastic coolant reservoirand, if necessary, add coolant.
Car Does Not: If your car does not have one of these reservoirs, you willneed to remove the radiator cap to check the fluid, but only ifthe engine is cool.
Wrap Cloth Thecap: To remove the cap, wrap a cloth around thecap and slowly loosen it to the first stop.

Air Intake Fuel: The air intake and fuel systems work together to createthis mixture.
Systems Seem Complex: These systems may seem complex, but they rely on three basicprinciples: air-fuel mixture, pressure, and gasoline vaporization.
Combustion Process Creates: The combustion process creates power byburning a mixture of air and gasoline.
step_by_step_procedure: AIR GAS RICHamounts: The AIR GAS RICHamounts of each, however, change all the time 8 TO 1 because of differences in temperature, vehiclespeed, and terrain.
Engine Burns Fuel: The engine burns fuel best, with the most complete combustion and thelowest emissions, when it mixes 14.7 parts of GASair with one part of gasoline.
Alean Mixture Air: Alean mixture, with more air and relatively less fuel (like a ratioof 17.0:1), may be all the car needs to cruise at low speed with a warm engine.
Air Inside Balloon: Air inside a balloon is under muchhigher pressure than air outside.

pamphlet_excerpts: Voltage Regulator Controls: A voltage regulator controls the amount of recharging.
Lighting System Includes: The lighting system includes the interior overhead lights, instrument lights, headlights, taillights, turn signals, warning lights, hazard lights.
Plunger-type Switches Close: When you open a car door, plunger-type switches close a circuit to the interior lights and make them go on.
Switch Underthe Pedal: When you apply the brakes, a switch underthe pedal closes a circuit to the brake light bulbs so they light up.
step_by_step_procedure: Wires Connect Battery: Wires connect the battery to many other accessories, includingthe sound system, heating and cooling systems, and (if the carhas them) power.
Cases Sound System: In some cases (such as the sound system and theheating and cooling systems), you must also turn the ignitionswitch on to close the circuit.
Solenoid Coil Wire: A solenoid is a coil of wire that wraps around a metalcore.
Electricity Magnetizes Coil: Electricity magnetizes the coil and makes the coremove, opening or closing an electrical circuit.

pamphlet_excerpts: Seen Idea Work: You may have seen this idea at work on a bicycle.
Yourchain Small Chain: If yourchain is on a small chain ring in the front and a large sprocketin the back, it will help you climb a very steep hill.
Large Chain Ring: If it is on a large chain ring and a small sprocket, it will help you pedalalong a flat road at high speed.
Key Difference Car: A key difference between a car transmission and a bicyclegear set is that on a bicycle, you can use any chain ring withany sprocket.
step_by_step_procedure: Car However Gears: On a car, however, the gears on the input shaft (coming from the engine) and the output shaft (going towardthe wheels) are always connected in pairs.
Time Shiftgears Transmission: Each time you shiftgears, the transmission tells a different pair of gears to sendpower to the wheels.
There Basic Types: There are two basic types of transmissions: manualand automatic.
Manual Transmission Shifting: With a manual transmission, just before shifting gears, thedriver must push a pedal down to release the clutch.

pamphlet_excerpts: Check Owner Smanual: Check the owner’smanual to learnhow to turn onthe lights for yourparticular vehicle.
Light Bulbs Car: Light bulbs in a car burn out just like the ones at home, andyou must replace them.
Check Lights Yourvehicle: You should check all the lights on yourvehicle from time to time to make sure they work properly.
Turn Headlights: Turn on the headlights, which will simultaneously light theinstrument lights and taillights.
step_by_step_procedure: Engage High Beams: Engage the high beams on the headlights and makesure that both headlights’ high beams work.
Friend Stepon Brake: Have a friend stepon the brake pedal while you check to see that the brake lightswork.
Friend Start Engine: Have your friend start the engine, applythe brakes, and shift into reverse while youcheck the backup lights.
Return Carto Park: Return the carto park and turn off then engine, thenturn on the hazard light switch andturn indicator.

Automotive Maintenance.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Determine the value of three different vehicles you are interested in purchasing. One must be new and one must be used; the third vehicle can be new or used. For each vehicle, find out the requirements and cost of automobile insurance to include basic liability and options for collision, comprehensive, towing, and rental car. Using the three vehicles you chose and with your counselor's assistance, complete the operation/maintenance chart provided in the Automotive Maintenance merit badge pamphlet. Use this information to determine the operating cost per mile for each vehicle, and discuss what you learn with your counselor. (b) Choose a car cleaner and wax product for a vehicle you want to clean. Explain clear-coat paint and the precautions necessary for care. Clean the vehicle, both inside and out, and wax the exterior. Use a vinyl and rubber protectant (on vinyl tops, rubber door seals, sidewalls, etc.) and explain the importance of this protectant. (c) Locate the manufacturer's jack. Use the jack to demonstrate how to engage the jack correctly on the vehicle, then change a tire correctly. (d) Perform an oil filter and oil change on a vehicle. Explain how to properly dispose of the used oil and filter.

Aviation.lead_text: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight. Do the following:
Aviation.req_text: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight. Do the following: (a) Define "aircraft." Describe three kinds of aircraft today, and their typical uses. (b) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of flight, and discuss three notable times in history important to aviation. (c) Explain the difference between a fixed wing and a rotary wing aircraft, and the benefits of each. (d) Explain the operation of piston, turbine, and jet engines. (e) Using a model aircraft, describe the four forces that act on an aircraft in flight. (f) Explain how an airfoil generates lift, specifically noting Bernoulli's principle. (g) Identify and describe the aerodynamic control surfaces on the aircraft of your choice, and explain how they operate to control its attitude and direction of flight. (h) Explain the purposes and functions of the various instruments found in a typical single-engine aircraft: attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator, turn and bank indicator, vertical speed indicator, compass, navigation, communication, and engine performance indicators.

step_by_step_procedure: Heading Indicator: The heading indicator can take differentforms but is basically a gyroscope thatshows the plane’s heading.

Aviation.lead_text: Flight Operations. Do TWO of the following:
Aviation.req_text: Flight Operations. Do TWO of the following: (a) Using a flight simulator software package, set a course and fly the headings you have established with a successful take-off and landing. (b) Under supervision, perform a preflight inspection of an aircraft. (c) Observe and/or participate in an aircraft maintenance activity. Describe the maintenance schedule and requirements for an aircraft of your choice. (d) Obtain and learn how to read an aeronautical chart. Measure a true course on the chart; correct it for magnetic variation, compass deviation, and wind drift to determine a navigational heading for an aircraft. (e) With your parent or guardian's permission, take a discovery flight in an aircraft. Record the date, place, type of aircraft, and duration of flight. Report on your impressions of the flight.

pamphlet_excerpts: Technicians Calculate: Technicians can calculate closely just how muchthe deviation will be for any airplane.
Aircraft Deviation Card: In every aircraft, you will find a deviation card mounted near the compass that tells us how to correct the magnetic coursefor deviation.
Remember Magnetic Course: Remember, the magnetic course from Indianapolis International (IND) to Crawfordsville Airport (CFJ) is 300 degrees.
Our Deviation Card: Our deviation card tells us that for a magnetic courseof 300 degrees, we should steer a course of 301 degrees.
step_by_step_procedure: Inother Words Compass: Inother words the compass deviation in our airplane at thiscourse is 1 degree higher than the magnetic course.
Now Proceed Steer: We can now proceed to steer at 301 degrees, confidentthat we will soon see the Crawfordsville Airport.
Requirement Learned Airspeed: For requirement 2(e), you learned that your airspeed indicatorshows how fast you are passing through the air, not over the ground.
Flying Knot Headwind: If you are flying into a 25-knot headwind, you areactually traveling over the ground at 25 knots less than yourairspeed.

Aviation.lead_text: Airport Operations. Do ONE of the following:
Aviation.req_text: Airport Operations. Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit an airport. After the visit, report on how the facilities are used, how runways are numbered, and how runways are determined to be "active." (b) Visit a Federal Aviation Administration facility: Airport Traffic Control Tower (ATCT), Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC), or Flight Standards District Office (FSDO). Report on the operation and your impressions of the facility. (c) Visit a military aviation facility. Learn how that facility supports defense and/or civilian activities. Report on the operation and your impressions of the facility. (d) Visit an aviation museum or attend an air show. Report on your impressions of the museum or show, and what you learned from the experience.

People Control Tower: The people in the control tower have four primary responsibilities.
Theactual TRACON Facility: Theactual TRACON facility might not be located in the controltower or even on the airport site.
step_by_step_procedure: Visit Terminal Radar: When you visit a terminal radar control facility, expectto enter a darkened room lit only by the glow of radarscreens.
Controllers Skillfully: Controllers skillfully observe and maneuverthe “blips” that appear on their screens; each blip represents an aircraft.
Ever Played Computer: If you have ever played a computer orvideo game, you have some idea of the intense natureof this responsibility.
Facilities Mentioned Welcome: Most of the facilities mentioned welcome visitors, and you can find theirphone numbers in your phone book.

pamphlet_excerpts: Recreationalpilot Certificatehas: The recreationalpilot certificatehas some importantrestrictions.
Mostimportantly Thepilot Fly: Mostimportantly, thepilot can fly onlyduring daylighthours and inairspace wherehe or she does notneed to communicate with airtraffic control.
Certificates Ratings: Of all the certificates and ratings, the recreational pilot certificateis the easiest to obtain.
Requires Hours Flight: It requires 30 hours of flight instruction (three hours of which must be solo flight time).
step_by_step_procedure: Recreationalpilot Earn: The recreationalpilot may earn additional privileges.
FAA Created Sport: The FAA created the sport pilot’s license in 2004 to help lowerthe barriers of entry-level aviation by making flying moreaffordable and accessible.
Enthusiast Light-sport: If you are an enthusiast of light-sport aircraft (LSA), consider a sport pilot certificateif you want to fly one.
Recreational Pilotcertificate: Like the recreational pilotcertificate, this certificate will allow the pilot to carry only onepassenger at up to 10,000 feet above sea.

pamphlet_excerpts: There Types Venomous: There are two types of venomous snakes in the United States.
Pit Vipers Rattlesnakes: Pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths) have triangular heads with pit marks on both sides ofthe head.
Coral Snakes Black: Coral snakes have black snouts and bands of red andyellow separated by bands of black.
Coral Snakes Injectpowerful: Coral snakes injectpowerful venom that works on the victim’s nervoussystem; pit-viper venom affects the circulatory system.
step_by_step_procedure: Hiking Stick Does: A hiking stick does double duty when youwalk through places where snakes might lurk.
Walk Slowly Stick: Walk slowly and use the stick to poke amongstones and brush ahead of you.
Whereyou Hands Collect: Watch whereyou put your hands as you collect firewoodor climb over rocks and logs.
Bite Nonvenomous Snake: The bite of a nonvenomous snake causes onlyminor puncture wounds.

pamphlet_excerpts: Pack Weighs Depends: How much your pack weighs depends on the length of the adventureyou have planned, the amount of food and equipment you must carry, and your personal.
Comfort Trail Pack: For comfort on the trail, a pack containing everything you need for a safe trek should tip the scale at no morethan 25 percent of your body’s weight.
Pack Weighs Here: If your pack weighs more, here are some tips for lighteningyour pack without compromising your health or safety. 1.
Shakedown Trip Shake: Do a shakedown before every trip to “shake out” everything youwon’t need. 2.
step_by_step_procedure: Divide Group Gear: Divide group gear so that each person carries a fair share. 3.
Gradually Replace Heavy: Gradually replace your heavy equipment and clothing with lighteritems.
Choose Lightweight Hiking: Choose lightweight hiking boots over stiff, heavy footwear. 5.
Prepare One-pot Meals: Prepare one-pot meals featuring pasta, powdered sauce mixes, andother ingredients that are dry, easy to pack, and not very heavy. 6.

pamphlet_excerpts: Extending Courtesy Outdoor: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habitof backpackers.
Carry Amobile Telephone: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off andstow it in your pack until you need it.
Appreciate Companyof Meet: Appreciate the companyof those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, butrespect their desire for quiet and solitude.
Encounter Horsebackriders: If you encounter horsebackriders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider what youshould do.
step_by_step_procedure: Lead Rider Probably: The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while theanimals pass.
Encounter Hikers: If you encounter other hikers or backpackersgoing uphill when you are going downhill, give them the rightof-way.
Aside Rock Log: Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact.
Possible Campaway Trailsand: If possible, campaway from trailsand other visitors.

pamphlet_excerpts: Minimizing Risk Caught: Minimizing Risk.
Metal Conducts Electricity: Metal conducts electricity, so avoid metal poles.
Astorm Catches Cave: If astorm catches you, find a cave or a low spot among the rocks.
Avoidprominent Outcroppings: Avoidprominent outcroppings, overhangs, and flood zones. • If you cannot find shelter, become the smallest target you can.
step_by_step_procedure: Notlie Flat Ground: Do notlie flat on the ground, because lying flat makes you a bigger target thancrouching down.
Less Touching Ground: The less of you that is touching the ground, the better.
Places Safe Chargestays: Such places are safe because the chargestays within the frame of the building or vehicle and is conducted safelyto ground without endangering.
Staying Near Stoves: Staying near stoves, fireplaces, and plumbing is alsodangerous, because metal can conduct electricity.

pamphlet_excerpts: Maps Compasses GPSreceivers: Maps, compasses, and GPSreceivers will be of little help ifyou don’t remember to usethem.
Secrets Safebackcountry: One of the secrets of safebackcountry hiking is the useof thumbnail navigation.
Technique Calls Yourconstant: This technique calls for yourconstant awareness of yourposition.
Carry Atopographic Map: You must carry atopographic map where youcan easily refer to it, that is, in your shirt or pants pocketrather than in your pack.
step_by_step_procedure: Hike Shouldcontinuously: As you hike, you shouldcontinuously try to matchup features around you withpoints on your map.
Not Prevent Getting: Not only will this prevent you from getting too far off yourroute if you take a wrong turn, it will keep your map-readingskills sharp.
Basic Knowledge Route: With a basic knowledge of route finding and theuse of thumbnail navigation, there is little chance of becomingtruly lost.
Determine Position Bestthing: If you find you can’t determine your position, the bestthing to do is stop walking.

pamphlet_excerpts: Getting Injured Out: Getting injured while out on the trail is one of the biggest risksfor which you need to be prepared.
Fortunately Trailinjuries: Fortunately, many trailinjuries, scrapes, bruises, blisters, and sunburn, usually arenot very troublesome.
Soap Water Bandages: Soap, water, bandages, and other itemsin your first-aid kit will take care of the majority of medicalproblems you may encounter.
However Danger Serious: However, the danger of a more serious injury is magnifiedby your distance from emergency response.
step_by_step_procedure: Miles Trail Rely: Miles up a trail, you must rely on your own resources and those of your companions.
Prevent Recognize Treat: Know how to prevent, recognize, and treat the healthhazards that may arise during a backpacking trip.
Briefdiscussions Follow: The briefdiscussions that follow are intended only to alert you to thedangers.
Consult First-aid Manual: Consult a first-aid manual for complete information.

pamphlet_excerpts: Follow Guidelines Safe: Follow these guidelines for the safe use of chemical-fuel stoves. 1.
Compressed- Liquid-gas: Use compressed- or liquid-gas stoves only with knowledgeable adultsupervision and only where and when permitted.
Home Store Fuelcontainers: At home, store fuelcontainers in a shed, garage, or other uninhabited structure. 2.
Read Understand Manufacturer: Read and understand the manufacturer’s instructions before lightingany stove.
step_by_step_procedure: Liquid Fuels Well-marked: Keep liquid fuels in well-marked, approved containers only and neverin a glass container.
Store Fuel Ventilated: Store fuel in a ventilated, locked box a minimumof 20 feet from buildings and tents.
Chemical-fuel Containersaway: Keep all chemical-fuel containersaway from stoves and campfires and store them below 100 degrees. 4.
Stove Cool Completely: Let a stove cool completely before changing cylinders of compressedgases, refilling from containers of liquid gas, and storing the stove.

pamphlet_excerpts: Extending Courtesy Outdoor: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habitof backpackers.
Carry Amobile Telephone: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off andstow it in your pack until you need it.
Appreciate Companyof Meet: Appreciate the companyof those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, butrespect their desire for quiet and solitude.
Encounter Horsebackriders: If you encounter horsebackriders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider what youshould do.
step_by_step_procedure: Lead Rider Probably: The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while theanimals pass.
Encounter Hikers: If you encounter other hikers or backpackersgoing uphill when you are going downhill, give them the rightof-way.
Aside Rock Log: Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact.
Possible Campaway Trailsand: If possible, campaway from trailsand other visitors.

Backpacking.req_text: Do the following: (a) Write a plan for a backpacking trek of at least five days using at least three different campsites and covering at least 30 miles. Your plan must include a description of and route to the trek area, a schedule (including a daily schedule), a list of food and equipment needs, a safety and emergency plan, and a budget. (b) Following the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code, take the trek as planned in requirement 11(a) that is at least five full days, covering at least 30 miles and utilizing at least three different campsites. While on trek, complete at least one service project approved by your counselor. (c) Keep a daily journal during the trek that includes a day-by-day description of your activities, including notes about what worked well and thoughts about improvements that could be made for the next trek.

pamphlet_excerpts: Common Weaves: The following are common weaves used in this pamphlet.
Over-under Weave Plainweave: Sometimes called over-under weave, the plainweave is done with rigid stakes or spokes, and weavers thatwrap around the stakes in an over-one.
Spokes Stakes Rigid: Spokes and stakes usually are more rigid and thicker reedthan weavers.
Continuous Weave Looks: Continuous weave looks much the same as plainweave, but it is woven with a different technique.
step_by_step_procedure: Weave Created Odd: This weave is created over an odd numberof stakes.
Not Done Row: It is not done one row at a time, but continuouslyfrom beginning to end, with additional weavers added whenmore length is needed.
Method Weaving Involves: This method of weaving involves the weaverpassing over two or more stakes and under two or more stakesat a time.
Weave Pairing Involvestwo: This weave, sometimes called pairing, involvestwo weavers, each alternately twisting over and underconsecutive spokes.

pamphlet_excerpts: Birds Lend Life: Birds lend life, color, and music to the outdoors, andthey are an important part of the ecosystems that keep thisplanet healthy.
They Sensitive Changes: Because they are sensitive to changes in theenvironment, birds are valuable indicators of trouble, includingpollution and habitat loss.
Near-disappearance Baldeagles: It was the near-disappearance of baldeagles, peregrine falcons, and brown pelicans decades ago thatalerted people to the dangers of many.
Major Rapiddeclines Number: Major, rapiddeclines in the number of songbirds have shown that we mustpreserve large areas for wildlife habitat.
step_by_step_procedure: Species Lumped Its: Each species is lumped with its closest relativesto form a genus, usually on the basis of physical characteristicslike the shapes of certain bones.
Closely Related Genera: Closely related genera (theplural of “genus”) are grouped together to form a family.
Field Guides Arranged: Most field guides are arranged inthis taxonomic order.
Related Birds Act: Because related birds often act and looksomewhat the same, knowing these relationshipscan help you identify a new, puzzling species.
